{{Short description|Geometric feature of pavement surfaces}}
[[File:Cross Slope.svg|thumb|upright=2.0|Cross section of a road. 1.&nbsp;Gutter; 2.&nbsp;Shoulder; 3.&nbsp;Sub-base; 4.&nbsp;Base&nbsp;course; 5.&nbsp;Asphalt]]
'''Cross slope''', '''cross fall''' or '''camber''' is a geometric feature of pavement surfaces: the transverse slope with respect to the horizon. It is a very important safety factor. Cross slope is provided to provide a [[drainage gradient]] so that water will run off the surface to a [[drainage]] system such as a [[street gutter]] or [[ditch]]. Inadequate cross slope will contribute to [[aquaplaning]]. On straight sections of normal two-lane roads, the pavement [[Cross section (geometry)|cross section]] is usually highest in the center and drains to both sides. In horizontal curves, the cross slope is banked into [[Cant (road/rail)|superelevation]] to reduce steering effort and lateral force required to go around the curve.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.tn.gov/content/dam/tn/tdot/roadway-design/documents/training/Superelevation%20Design%20Guide.pdf|title=Superelevation Design Guide|author=Department of Transportation|date=23 January 2023}}</ref>  All water drains to the inside of the curve.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://wsdot.wa.gov/publications/manuals/fulltext/M22-01/1250.pdf|title=Cross Slope and Superelevation|author=WSDOT|date=23 January 2023}}</ref> If the cross slope magnitude oscillates within {{convert|1|-|25|m|ft|0}}, the body and payload of high (heavy) vehicles will experience high roll and lateral vibration.

Cross slope is usually expressed as a percentage:
:<math>\text{cross slope} = \frac{\text{rise}}{\text{run}} \times 100\%</math>.

Cross slope is the angle around a vertical axis between:
* the horizontal line that is perpendicular to the road's center line, and
* the surface.

Typical values range from 2 percent for straight segments to 10 percent for sharp superelevated curves. It may also be expressed as a fraction of an inch in rise over a one-[[Foot (unit)|foot]] run (e.g. {{frac|1|4}}&nbsp;inch&nbsp;per&nbsp;foot).
